original_value: Cloud computing has been widely adopted to support various computation services. A fundamental problem faced by cloud providers is how to efficiently allocate resources upon user requests and price the resource usage, in order to maximize resource efficiency and hence provider profit. Existing studies establish detailed performance models of cloud resource usage, and propose offline or online algorithms to decide allocation and pricing. Differently, we adopt a blackbox approach, and leverage model-free Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) to capture dynamics of cloud users and better characterize inherent connections between an optimal allocation/pricing policy and the states of the dynamic cloud system. The goal is to learn a policy that maximizes net profit of the cloud provider through trial and error, which is better than decisions made on explicit performance models. We combine long short-term memory (LSTM) units with fully-connected neural networks in our DRL to deal with online user arrivals, and adjust the output and update methods of basic DRL algorithms to address both resource allocation and pricing. Evaluation based on real-world datasets shows that our DRL approach outperforms basic DRL algorithms and state-of-theart white-box online cloud resource allocation/pricing algorithms significantly, in terms of both profit and the number of accepted users.

result.paraphrase: Cloud computing is now widely used to deliver a range of computation services. For cloud providers, a key challenge is allocating resources efficiently in response to user requests while also pricing resource use so as to maximize efficiency and, in turn, profit. Prior work has built detailed performance models for cloud resource consumption and has proposed offline and online methods for allocation and pricing decisions. In contrast, we take a black-box approach and use model-free Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) to capture cloud-user dynamics and better represent the relationship between an optimal allocation/pricing policy and the state of the evolving cloud system. Our objective is to learn, through trial and error, a policy that maximizes the cloud provider’s net profit, rather than relying on decisions derived from explicit performance models. To handle online user arrivals, we integrate long short-term memory (LSTM) units with fully connected neural networks in our DRL framework, and we modify the output and update procedures of standard DRL algorithms to support both resource allocation and pricing. Experiments on real-world datasets show that our DRL method significantly outperforms baseline DRL algorithms and state-of-the-art white-box online cloud resource allocation/pricing methods in both profit and the number of accepted users.
